en: Abhidhānottara 10 = palm-leaf manuscript = Lokesh Chandra’s reproduction of Raghu Vīra’s manuscript.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the ritual procedure for the Pure Seat (śuddhapīṭha)—
the supreme secret, the most profound mystery, the heart of the ḍākinīs,
the yoga that is the abode of all mantras, and the bestower of all accomplishments.

Then all those Tathāgatas, the great lords of the vajra-yoga, together with their retinues and assemblies, and the hosts of great Ḍākas and Ḍākinīs, again prostrated before the Blessed One, the Great Samantabhadra, the Great Vajradhara, the Lord, and spoke as follows:
Oh, supreme among those whose nature is passion! Oh, charioteer of passion!
Speak the secret mandala, the most excellent assembly of dakinis.
Speak of the Buddha-yoga and the unsurpassed Vajra-yoga; speak of the secret mandala that brings about the bliss of the three realms,
which consists of the universal vajra-jewel and sets in motion the yoga of the universe.
Speak of the pure maṇḍala arising from Vajrabhairava:
a delightful city, square in shape, endowed with four gates,
complete with every ornament, the maṇḍala born of the supreme rapture.
In the center there is a double wheel, the supreme sequence of mind and speech;
it has eight spokes, appears blue and red, and is adorned with a garland of vajras and lotuses.
Having surrounded the mandala, the supreme of mandalas, with a circle of wheels on the outside,
one should [surround] its exterior with the Viśvayoginī through her transformations of dance and song.
And on the outside, a garland of pretas of various excellent colors,
performing dances and brandishing their hands, with distorted faces that are licking [their lips].
In the center there should be an empty space, with the supreme syllable *HŪṂ* as the moon;
transforming that, one should visualize the excellent Vajra and Vajrasattva.
He has three faces, six arms, and three eyes, and is the essence of compassion;
he is absorbed in the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) and is firmly seated in the vajra posture.
Seated upon a lion-throne in the lotus posture, situated in the midst of a lunar mandala,
his faces are white, blue, and reddish-brown, born from the vajras of body, speech, and mind.
Holding a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga staff, he embraces a vajra and a bell;
he holds a hand-drum and a human head, with Akṣobhya as his crest-jewel.
The arrangement of the *ḍākinī* seats and likewise the arrangement of the heroes;
the elements, aggregates, and sense-bases; the cultivation of body, speech, and mind;
and the goddess who manifests in that form, bringing the bliss of Mahāmudrā.
In the heart, however, is the seed-syllable Maṃ in the center of a moon-maṇḍala.
One should recollect the mantra of the primordial siddha accompanied by two *hoḥ* syllables;
this mudrā, when sealed, resides in the heart-lotus and in the secret place.
O Śānta, O Takṣaṇa, may she be dear to the God, gentle and devoted;
O Lord of Passion, Great Master, [unite] with your own Vajrasattva through the desire for bliss.
By means of that, one becomes a great player in these [realms] through the union of the two organs;
yet both, being unable to endure it, go to the abode of pleasure.
Immediately upon arising, the Vajrayoginīs urged them on with the sound of damaru drums and bells.
Through the union of the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*), they attained great bliss (*mahāsukha*).

Then all those Tathāgatas, equal in number to the atoms of the entire realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), together with their retinues, surrounded by the secret heroes (*vīra*) and ḍākinīs, preceded by the assembly of Bodhisattvas, and encompassing the hosts of ḍākinīs without exception or remainder, as well as the expansion of external and internal male and female messengers (*dūta-dūtī*), were struck with extreme wonder. Suddenly, out of joy, they performed graceful dances with playful gestures.
Placing their joined palms together at their heads, they pay homage;
they satisfy him with this song, and then:
"Oh, what a most wonderful Dharma! Oh, what a most wonderful conduct!"
Oh, what a most wonderful secret! Oh, the source of bliss!
Oh, the meaning of Samantabhadra! Oh, the union of passion!
Oh, the great purity of happiness! Oh, the supreme happiness of happiness!
Oh, the union with mantra! Oh, the accumulation of the heart-essence!
Oh, the attainment of the mudrā! Oh, the marvelous sādhana!
Oh, the boundless stage! Oh, how they follow accordingly!
Oh, the great body of the universe! Oh, the purity of the triple-enveloping!
Oh, the union of the vajra! Oh, the lotus-apertures!
Oh, the union of the two organs! Oh, the supreme bliss, which is equanimous!
Oh, how pure is the vocal music today! Oh, how stainless is the song! Oh, the excellence of the instrumental accompaniment! Oh, the rhythm that dispels all discord!
Oh, how beautiful is the array of flowers! Oh, how auspicious is the incense burner!
Oh, the island that destroys darkness! Oh, the fragrance so cool!
Oh, the union with the yogins! Oh, illusion, comparable to a womb!
Oh, to the supreme Vajra of the Buddhas! Oh, the supreme Jewel, the bestower of bliss!
Oh, the savior of Padmāvatī! Oh, the miraculous manifestation of Viśvamāyā!
Oh, the wonder of the Buddhas! Oh, the wonder of the Śauris!
Oh, the wonder of sentient beings! Oh, the wonder of the deities!
Urged by this, the Lord manifested the supreme seed-syllable,
possessing the radiant color of saffron, well-arisen with the vajra as its emblem,
six-faced, twelve-armed, and beautifully adorned by Vārāhī.
Accompanied by his consort, the Great Hero, seated comfortably in the half-lotus posture,
three-eyed, smiling, fierce, formidable, and loathsome, with a tongue lolling out, he is the essence of compassion.
Bhairava and Kālarātri stand beneath the soles of his feet; moreover,
he is established in the ālīḍha posture, performing a most wondrous act of creation,
situated upon a lotus atop the orb of the moon.
The color of its nine filaments is that of the mudrā, adorned with that same color;
blue, green, yellow, and red for the sake of pacifying [the afflictions], while white is for peace.
It has a crown of skulls as a diadem, beautified by the images of the Buddhas.
He is in union with the Vajra-bell, pressed against the breasts of the goddess;
having cut off external patience, his body is turned backward,
and he stands with his waist encircled by the skin of a fierce Bhairava.
She holds a skull-cup and a khaṭvāṅga, and likewise wields a sword, an utpala lotus,
a goad, a noose, a ḍamaru drum, a severed head, and a bow;
she possesses these faces and weapons, and stands in the state of Great Passion with Vārāhī.
Embraced by her two shanks, she is a beautiful woman of great passion;
her body is fierce with a garland of severed heads, and she is adorned with the marks of the six mudrās.
Thus the mantra practitioner meditates upon Mañjuvajra, the Great Bliss;
by means of the yoga of the seats and so forth, he [becomes] the Lord of Wisdom in every respect. Through the yoga of the *ḍākinī* net, he attains the *saṃvara*, the supreme *saṃvara*.

First, on the eastern spoke of the mind-wheel (*cittacakra*) at Pullīramalaya, Khaṇḍakapālin and Pracaṇḍā are white, blue, and green. On the northern [spoke] at Jālandhara, Mahākaṅkāla and Caṇḍākṣī are yellow, blue, and green.
In Oḍiyāna in the west is Kaṅkālaprabhāvatī, red, yellow, and green.
In Arbuda in the south is Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrimahānāsā, green, yellow, and red.
In Godāvarī in the southeast is Surāvairiṇavīramatī, red, yellow, and green.
In the southwest, at Rāmeśvara, is Amitābhakharvarī, who is white, yellow, and green.
In the northwest, at Devikoṭa, is Vajraprabhalaṅkeśvarī, who is sky-colored, white, yellow, and green.
In the northeast, at Mālava, is Vajradehadrumacchāyā, who is green, red, and blue.
In the mind wheel (cittacakra), the heroes such as Khaṇḍakapāla and others hold vajras and vajra-bells while embracing [their consorts] such as Pracaṇḍā and others.
In the second, the speech-wheel (*vākcakra*),
on the eastern spoke at Kāmarūpa are Aṅkurikā and Airāvatī, white, blue, and green;
on the northern spoke at Oḍra are Vajrajaṭilā and Mahābhairavā, green, yellow, and blue.
In the west, at Triśakuni, Mahāvīravāyuvegā is blue, yellow, and green;
in the south, at Kośalā, Vajrahūṃkārasurābhakṣī is red, yellow, and green;
in the southeast, at Kaliṅga, Subhadraśyāmādevī is green, yellow, and blue.
In the southwest, at Lampāka, are Vajrabhadra and Subhadrā, who are yellow, blue, and green;
in the northwest, at Kāñcī, are Mahābhairava and Hayakarṇā, who are smoky-grey, grey, yellow, and blue;
in the northeast, at Himālaya, are Virūpākṣa and Khagānanā, who are sky-colored, white, yellow, and green.
In the speech-wheel (vākcakra), there are Aṅkurikā, Airāvatī, Āliṅganā, Padmā, and Ghaṇṭādhara.
Thus, there are two wheels: Khecarī and Bhūcarī.
In the third [mandala], which arises from the body-wheel (*kāyacakra*), there is a square with four gates.
At the eastern gate, in Pretapurī, are Mahābalā and Cakravegā, who are blue, yellow, and green.
At the northern gate, in Gṛhadevatā, are Ratnavajrā and Khaṇḍarohā, who are yellow, blue, and green.
At the western gate, in Saurāṣṭra, there is Hayagrīva and Śauṇḍinī, who are red, yellow, and green.

At the southern gate, in Suvarṇadvīpa, there is Ākāśagarbha and Cakravartinī, who are white, blue, and green. In the southeast, in Nagara, there is Śrī Heruka and Suvīrā, who are sky-blue, yellow, and green.
In the southwest, at Sindhū, Padmanarteśvara and Mahābalā are red, yellow, and green;
in the northwest, at Maru, Vairocana and Cakravarmiṇī are white, blue, and green;
in the northeast, at Kulatā, Vajrasattva and Mahāvīryā are white, blue, and green.
In the body wheel (*kāyacakra*), there are Mahābalā and the others, who hold wheels and bells while embracing Cakravega and the others.

All these heroes have three faces and six arms; they stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, possess three eyes, and hold in their hands a skull-cup (*kapāla*), a khatvāṅga staff, a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*), and a curved knife (*kartti*).
Just as the heroes are characterized by the color and insignia of their arms, so too should the ḍākinīs and others be depicted.
They all possess vajra-bodies, wear garlands of skulls and crowns, have their heads adorned by the lords of their respective families, bear the five mudrās, and are girt with tiger-skin loincloths.
The goddesses indeed have their hair loose and are entwined with pairs of vajras and bells;
they all wear no clothes and are hideous, fierce, and terrifying.
In the center, indeed, is Mañjuvajra, auspicious and bearing a crescent moon;
his crown is pressed down by a double vajra (viśvavajra). Vārāhī has disheveled hair, is naked, and her girdle is adorned with bone fragments.
Having drawn forth the wheel of gnosis (jñānacakra) according to the sequence of the previously mentioned ritual procedure, [one should join it].
One should practice the state of empowerment within the entry into the state of equanimity (*samarasībhāva*). Having sequentially traversed all the seats (*pīṭha*) from the [central] seat,
one should [realize] the supreme mind, speech, and body, which are the elements, aggregates, and sense-bases.
One should contemplate the stage of consecration, the pledge of gnosis, within the heart.
Thereafter, having performed the placement of the armor (*kavaca*), the wise one should recite the mantra of gnosis.
By means of the excellent machine of breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should recite the visualization of the meditative state.
Oṃ āḥ maṃ hūṃ.
One should recite [the mantra] devoid of the sky through the yoga of emanation and reabsorption.
Then, one should perform the recitation of the Samayasattva according to the ritual procedure:
OṂ MAṂ MAÑJUVAJRADHṚK Ā HŪṂ HŪṂ ḌĀKINĪJĀLASAṂVARA HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ.
Oṃ vajravārāhī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā.
Oṃ kara 2 khaṇḍakapālina hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ pracaṇḍe hūṃ phūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kuru 2 mahākaṅkāla hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ caṇḍākṣī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bandha 2 kaṅkāla hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ prabhāvatī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ, terrify, terrify! O you with formidable fangs, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ, O Mahānāsa, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, agitate, agitate! O enemy of the gods, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ vīramatī hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hroṃ hoṃ amitābha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kharvarī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ hraḥ hraḥ vajraprabha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ laṅkeśvarī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ heṃ heṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ drumacchāye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ phaṭ 2 aṅkurike hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ airāvatī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |

Oṃ vāyuvege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ bhakṣa 2 vajrahūṃkāra vasarudhirāntramālāvalambine hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ surābhakṣī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ, seize, seize! O Subhadra, threaten all the serpents dwelling in the seven netherworlds! Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Śyāmādevī, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Ākaḍḍha Vajrabhadra, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ subhadre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hrīḥ hrīḥ mahābhairava hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hayakarṇe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ jñoṃ jñoṃ Virūpākṣa hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ Khagānane hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ kṣmāṃ 2 Mahābala hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ cakravege hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ ratnavajra hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ khaṇḍarohe hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ hīṃ 2 Hayagrīva hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ nī [? hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hūṃ hūṃ Ākāśagarbha hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ cakravartinī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ kili 2 heruka hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ (*47r) suvīre hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ sili padmanarteśvara hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahābale hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ hili 2 vairocana hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
Oṃ cakravarmiṇī hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ dhili 2 vajrasattva hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ | Oṃ mahāvīrye hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ |
One should recite the mantra according to the prescribed rite using a large conch-shell rosary,
devoted to the practice of recitation and meditation throughout the four junctions of the day.
The yogi shall indeed attain accomplishment without delay through the sequence of mantra-accomplishment;
the practitioner of mantra should constantly worship himself as joined with the mudrā.
Having entered the mandala, the mantra-practitioner, through the meditations on body, speech, and mind,
and by means of the yoga with his own tutelary deity, [attains] the supreme mandala of accomplishment,
which bestows all accomplishments through the yoga with the deities of the mandala.
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the Mañjuvajra-vidhi-paṭala, concerning the three wheels, in the Abhidhānottara.
